{"slug": "how-to-write-a-great-ai-website-prompt", "title": "How to Write a Great AI Website Prompt (2026 Guide)", "metaTitle": "How to Write a Great AI Website Prompt (2026 Guide)", "metaDescription": "Learn the 4 things every AI website prompt needs, see bad-vs-good examples, and get 3 full prompts you can copy and adapt in Kodely.", "targetKeyword": "how to write a great AI website prompt", "category": "Guides", "bodyHtml": "

Type “build me a bakery website” into an AI website builder and you will get a website. It will have a hero section, some cards, a muted color palette, and absolutely nothing that makes it yours. The tool did exactly what you asked — it just didn’t know anything about your bakery, because you didn’t tell it anything.

The gap between a generic result and a genuinely usable one isn’t the AI model. It’s the prompt. This guide walks through what a strong prompt actually contains, shows a bad prompt rewritten into a good one, and gives you full examples you can adapt right now.

Why vague prompts produce generic results

An AI website builder like Kodely has to fill in every blank you leave open. Who is this site for? What pages does it need? What should it feel like — playful, corporate, minimal? If you don’t answer these, the model picks the statistically safest defaults: a hero, three feature cards, a testimonials strip, a contact form. That’s not a failure of the tool. It’s the predictable result of an underspecified request.

The fix isn’t a longer prompt for its own sake. It’s a prompt that removes the guesswork on the handful of decisions that actually shape the output.

The 4 things every good prompt should include

You don’t need a novel. You need these four things, in whatever order feels natural to write:

  • Who it’s for. The business or person, and ideally the audience they’re trying to reach. “A landscaping company” is thinner than “a landscaping company targeting homeowners in suburban neighborhoods.”
  • The sections or pages needed. Don’t make the AI guess your site structure. List them: a homepage with services and a quote form, an about page, a gallery of past projects.
  • Tone and style. Bold and modern? Warm and approachable? Minimal and text-heavy? One or two adjectives plus a reference point (“like a boutique studio, not a big-box chain”) goes a long way.
  • One concrete detail. A real business name, an actual color, a specific line of copy, a real neighborhood. Concrete details anchor the output in something specific instead of something templated — this is the single highest-leverage addition you can make to a prompt.

Bad prompt vs. good rewrite

Bad promptGood rewrite
Make me a website for a coffee shop.Build a homepage for Marlowe & Finch, a small-batch coffee roaster in a converted warehouse space. Sections: hero with our tagline “Roasted Tuesdays, Served All Week,” a menu section with 3 drink categories, a short story about our roasting process, and a location/hours block. Warm, industrial tone — think exposed brick and dark wood, not bright and cheerful. Use a deep amber and charcoal color scheme.
I need a portfolio site.Build a portfolio site for Dana Reyes, a freelance motion designer. Homepage needs a hero with my name and one-line pitch, a grid of 6 project thumbnails, a short bio section, and a contact section with my email. Tone: confident and minimal, dark background with a single bright accent color like electric blue. No stock-photo feel — treat it like a design agency’s own site.

Three example prompts you can adapt

A local service business: “Build a site for Ridgeline Home Repair, a general contractor serving the northern suburbs. Pages: a homepage with hero, a services list (roofing, drywall, kitchen remodels), a before/after project gallery, and a contact page with a quote request form. Tone should feel trustworthy and no-nonsense — plain language, not salesy. Use navy blue and white as the base colors, with the tagline ‘Fixed right, the first time.’”

A product landing page: “Build a landing page for Fernweg, a travel journaling app. One long homepage: hero with app screenshot placeholder and headline, a 3-step ‘how it works’ section, a features grid of 4 items, a pricing section with a free and a paid plan, and a footer with a signup form. Tone: warm and adventurous, not corporate SaaS. Use a terracotta and cream color palette.”

A personal brand/creator site: “Build a site for Theo Okafor, a woodworking YouTuber. Homepage needs a hero with a bold headline, an embedded-style video section (use a placeholder), a shop section previewing 3 physical products, and an about section with my background. Tone: rustic and handmade, not polished tech. Use deep walnut brown and off-white, and include the line ‘Built by hand, one board at a time.’”

How to iterate afterward

Once the first version is live in preview, resist the urge to rewrite the whole prompt from scratch. Kodely edits the real components that already exist, so the fastest path to the site you want is describing the specific change: “make the hero headline larger and center it,” “change the accent color to forest green,” “add a testimonials section between the services and the gallery.” Each of these becomes a checkpoint, so if an edit doesn’t land the way you wanted, rolling back to the previous version is free — you lose nothing by experimenting.

Common mistakes

  • Piling on requirements in one giant prompt. Start with the core structure, then layer in refinements one at a time — it’s easier to see what each change actually did.
  • Skipping the concrete detail. A prompt with no real name, color, or line of copy will always read as a placeholder site, no matter how detailed the rest of it is.
  • Describing implementation instead of outcome. Say what the section should communicate, not vague technical instructions — the model handles the how.
  • Restarting instead of iterating. If 80% of the site works, describe the 20% that doesn’t. Restarting throws away everything that was already right.

FAQ

Do I need to know how to code to write a good prompt? No. A good prompt is plain English with specific details — who the site is for, what it needs, and what it should feel like. Kodely turns that into a real Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind app behind the scenes.

How long should my first prompt be? A few sentences covering the four essentials — audience, sections, tone, and one concrete detail — is enough. You can always refine after seeing the live preview.

What if I don’t like the first result? Describe the specific change you want in chat rather than starting over. Every generation is a checkpoint, so you can also roll back to an earlier version for free if an edit takes things the wrong way.

Can I see the actual code it generates? Yes. Kodely’s code view shows the real component files it built, and you can copy them directly in-app.

The best way to get good at this is to try it. Try it now on Kodely, free — 750 credits, no credit card required.
